title: A custom of the isle of Cea
paragraphs: [Cos. Cea is the form of the name given by Pliny.]

If to philosophise is, as it is defined, to doubt, then much more should writing at random and playing the fool, as I do, be reckoned doubting; for it is for novices and freshmen to inquire and dispute, and for the chairman to moderate and decide.
My moderator is the authority of the divine will, which governs us without contradiction, and is seated above these human and vain disputations.

When Philip had forcibly entered the Peloponnese and someone said to Damidas that the Lacedaemonians stood likely to suffer greatly if they did not in time reconcile themselves to his favour, "Why, you wretched fellow," he replied, "what can they suffer who do not fear to die?" Agis, too, was asked how a man might live free. "Why," he said, "by despising death." These, and a thousand other sayings to the same effect, plainly mean more than patiently awaiting the stroke of death when it comes — for there are several accidents of life worse to suffer than death itself. Witness the Lacedaemonian boy captured by Antigonus and sold as a slave who, when his master ordered him to some base task, said, "You shall see whom you have bought — it would be a shame for me to serve, when liberty is within my reach," and so saying, threw himself from the top of the house. When Antipater severely threatened the Lacedaemonians, the better to bring them to grant a demand of his, they replied, "If you threaten us with worse than death, we shall die more willingly"; and to Philip, who had written that he would frustrate all their undertakings, "What, will you also stop us from dying?" This is the meaning of the saying that the wise man lives as long as he ought, not as long as he can; and that the most obliging present nature has given us, and which removes all colour for complaining of our condition, is that she has placed the keys of life in our own keeping. She has provided only one door into life, but a hundred thousand ways out. We may be cramped for earth to live on, but earth enough to die on can never be wanting, as Boiocalus answered the Romans. Why complain of this world? It does not detain you; your own cowardice is the cause if you live in pain. There needs no more to die than to will to die:
"Ubique mors est; optime hoc cavit deus. Eripere vitam nemo non homini potest; At nemo mortem; mille ad hanc aditus patent."
["Death is everywhere: heaven has well provided for that. Anyone can deprive us of life; no one can deprive us of death. To death there are a thousand approaches." — Seneca, Thebais, i. 151.]

Nor is it a remedy for one disease only; death is the sure cure of all. It is a most assured harbour that is never to be feared and very often to be sought. It is all one whether a man gives himself his end or waits to receive it by some other means — whether he pays before his day or stays till his day of payment comes; from wherever it comes, it is still his. In whatever part the thread breaks, that is the end of the skein. The most voluntary death is the finest. Life depends on the pleasure of others; death on our own. We should suit ourselves in nothing so much as in this. Reputation is not concerned in such an undertaking; it is folly to be troubled by any such worry. Living is slavery if the freedom to die is lacking. The ordinary cure is carried on at the expense of life: they torment us with cauteries, incisions, and amputations; they cut off our food and drain our blood; one step further and we are cured indeed and effectively. Why is not the jugular vein as much at our disposal as the median? For a desperate disease, a desperate cure. Servius the grammarian, tormented with gout, could think of no better remedy than to apply poison to his legs, to take away their feeling; let them be gouty all they liked, so long as they were insensible of pain. God gives us leave enough to go when He is pleased to reduce us to a condition in which to live is far worse than to die. It is weakness to give in to infirmities, but it is madness to feed them. The Stoics say that to take one's leave of life, even at the height of prosperity, is living according to nature in a wise man, if he does it at the right moment — and in a fool it is to prolong life, though he be miserable, provided he is not in want of the things they reckon to be according to nature. As I do not break the law against thieves when I help myself to my own money and cut my own purse, nor that against arsonists when I burn my own wood, so I am not under the lash of laws against murderers for having deprived myself of my own life. Hegesias said that just as the condition of life did, so the condition of death ought to depend on our own choice. And Diogenes, meeting the philosopher Speusippus, so swollen with a chronic dropsy that he had to be carried in a litter, and greeted by him with the polite "I wish you good health," replied, "No health to you, who are content to live in such a condition."
And in fact, not long afterwards, Speusippus, weary of so languishing a life, found a means to die.

But this does not pass without dispute. Many are of opinion that we cannot quit this garrison of the world without the express command of Him who placed us in it; and that it is for God, who has placed us here, not just for ourselves but for His glory and the service of others, to dismiss us when it best pleases Him, and not for us to depart without His leave; that we are not born only for ourselves but for our country also, the laws of which require an account from us for the sake of their own interest and have an action of manslaughter against us; and that if these fail to take cognisance of the act, we are punished in the other world as deserters of our duty:
"Proxima deinde tenent maesti loca, qui sibi letum Insontes peperere manu, lucemque perosi Proiecere animas."
["In the next region the sad ones dwell, who, though free from guilt, slew themselves by their own hand and, hating the light, cast away their lives." — Aeneid, vi. 434.]

There is more constancy in bearing the chain we are tied to than in breaking it, and more telling evidence of fortitude in Regulus than in Cato; it is indiscretion and impatience that push us to these precipices. No misfortune can make true virtue turn her back; she seeks and demands evils, pains, and griefs, as the things by which she is nourished and sustained. The threats of tyrants, racks, and tortures serve only to rouse and quicken her:
"Duris ut ilex tonsa bipennibus Nigrae feraci frondis in Algido, Per damma, percmdes, ab ipso Ducit opes, animumque ferro."
["As on Mount Algidus, the sturdy oak draws fresh vigour and spirit from the very axe that prunes it." — Horace, Od., iv. 4, 57.]
And as another says:
"Non est, ut putas, virtus, pater, Timere vitam; sed malis ingentibus Obstare, nec se vertere, ac retro dare."
["Father, it is not virtue, as you suppose, to fear life, but to stand up to great misfortunes, not to turn and run from them." — Seneca, Thebais, i. 190.]
Or as this:
"Rebus in adversis facile est contemnere mortem Fortius ille facit, qui miser esse potest."
["In adversity it is easy to despise death; he acts more bravely who can endure being wretched." — Martial, xi. 56, 15.]
It is cowardice, not virtue, to lie crouched in a furrow under a tomb to dodge the blows of fortune. Virtue never stops, never strays from her path, for the greatest storm that blows:
"Si fractus illabatur orbis, Impavidum ferient ruinae."
["Should the world's axis crack, the ruins will only crush a fearless head." — Horace, Od., iii. 3, 7.]
More often, fleeing other troubles brings us to this one; in trying to dodge death, we often run straight into its jaws:
"Hic, rogo, non furor est, ne moriare, mori?"
["Tell me, is it not madness to die for fear of dying?" — Martial, ii. 80, 2.]
— like those who, for fear of a precipice, throw themselves headlong into it:
"Multos in summa pericula misfit Venturi timor ipse mali: fortissimus ille est, Qui promptus metuenda pati, si cominus instent, Et differre potest."
["The fear of future evils often drives men into extreme danger; he is truly brave who boldly faces the troubles he dreads, when they confront him and can be put off." — Lucan, vii. 104.]
"Usque adeo, mortis formidine, vitae Percipit humanos odium, lucisque videndae, Ut sibi consciscant moerenti pectore lethum Obliti fontem curarum hunc esse timorem."

["So far does dread of death produce in some men a hatred of life and of seeing the light that they kill themselves with grieving hearts, forgetting that this very fear is the source of their cares." — Lucretius, iii. 79.]

Plato, in his Laws, assigns an ignominious burial to the man who has deprived his nearest and best friend — namely himself — of life and his allotted course, not being compelled to do so by public judgment, by any sad and inescapable accident of fortune, nor by any unbearable disgrace, but merely driven on by cowardice and the feebleness of a fearful soul. And the opinion that makes so little of life is ridiculous, for it is our being — it is all we have. Things of a higher and more elevated existence may, indeed, look down on ours, but it is against nature for us to despise and discount ourselves. It is a disease peculiar to man, not found in any other creature, to hate and despise itself. And it is a vanity of the same kind to want to be something other than we are; the effect of such a wish does not even touch us, since it is contradicted and frustrated in itself. He who asks to be turned from a man into an angel does nothing for himself; he would be no better off for it, since, being no more, who would there be left to rejoice or be aware of this benefit on his behalf?
"Debet enim, misere cui forti, aegreque futurum est, Ipse quoque esse in eo turn tempore, cum male possit Accidere."
["For the man who is to suffer misery and pain in the future must himself still exist at the time when these ills are to befall him." — Lucretius, ibid., 874.]

Security, indolence, freedom from feeling, the absence of the ills of this life — which we pretend to buy at the price of dying — are no advantage to us. The man who escapes war to no purpose, if he cannot enjoy peace, and just as little to the purpose, the man who escapes trouble who cannot enjoy rest.

Among those of the first of these two opinions, there has been great debate as to what occasions are sufficient to justify deliberate self-murder, which they call "a reasonable exit." For though they say that men must sometimes die for trivial causes, since those that detain us in life are of no great weight either, yet there must be some limit. There are fantastic and senseless impulses that have driven not only individual men but whole nations to destroy themselves, of which I have given examples elsewhere. We also read of the Milesian virgins, who by a mad compact hanged themselves one after another until the magistrate took order in it, decreeing that the bodies of any found so hanged should be drawn naked through the city by the same halter. When Therykion tried to persuade Cleomenes to dispatch himself because of the ill posture of his affairs and, having missed a more honourable death in the lost battle, to accept this second-best one rather than give the conquerors leisure to inflict on him either a shameful death or a degrading life, Cleomenes, with a courage truly Stoic and Lacedaemonian, rejected his advice as unmanly and base: "That," he said, "is a remedy that will never be unavailable, but one a man should not resort to while an inch of hope remains." He told him that it was sometimes constancy and valour to live; that he wanted even his death to be of use to his country, and would make of it an act of honour and virtue. Therykion, nevertheless, thought himself in the right and did his own business; and Cleomenes did the same afterwards, but only after he had first tried out the utmost malice of fortune. Not all the troubles in the world are weighty enough to make a man die to dodge them; and besides, there are so many sudden and unexpected changes in human affairs that it is hard to judge rightly when we are at the end of our hope:
"Sperat et in saeva victus gladiator arena, Sit licet infesto pollice turba minax."
["Even the conquered gladiator in the cruel arena still hopes, though the threatening crowd, with thumb turned down, orders him to die." — Pentadius, De Spe, in Virgilii Catalecta.]

All things, says an old adage, are to be hoped for by a man while he lives. Yes — but, replies Seneca, why should it run more in a man's head that fortune can do all things for the living man, than this: that fortune has no power over the man who knows how to die? Josephus, engaged in such near and obvious danger, with a whole people violently set against him and no visible means of escape, was, as he himself tells us, advised by one of his friends in this extremity to dispatch himself. It was well for him that he still kept up hope, for fortune diverted the danger beyond all human expectation, and he saw himself delivered without any harm. Whereas Brutus and Cassius, on the contrary, threw away the last remains of Roman liberty, of which they were the sole protectors, by the haste and rashness with which they killed themselves before the proper time and a just occasion. Monsieur d'Anguien, at the battle of Cerisoles, twice tried to run himself through, despairing of the day, which was going very badly on that side of the field where he was engaged, and by that haste came very close to depriving himself of the enjoyment of so brave a victory. I have seen a hundred hares escape from the very teeth of the greyhounds:
"Aliquis carnifici suo superstes fuit."
["Some men have outlived their executioner." — Seneca, Ep., 13.]
"Multa dies, variusque labor mutabilis nevi Rettulit in melius; multos alterna revisens Lusit, et in solido rursus fortuna locavit."

["Length of days, and the changing labour of fickle time, have brought things back to a better state; fortune, returning by turns, has toyed with many and set them again on firm ground." — Aeneid, xi. 425.]
Pliny says there are only three sorts of diseases that give a man fair title to destroy himself; the worst of which is the stone in the bladder, when the urine is blocked.

[In the 1588 quarto edition of these essays, Pliny is said to mention two more — a pain in the stomach and a headache — which, he says (lib. xxv. c. 9), were almost the only three diseases for which men killed themselves.]

Seneca says only those which keep on disturbing the functions of the soul for a long time. And there have been some who, to avoid a worse death, have chosen one of their own liking. Democritus, general of the Aetolians, brought as a prisoner to Rome, found a way to escape by night; but, hotly pursued by his keepers, he fell on his own sword and died rather than let himself be retaken. Antinous and Theodotus, when their city of Epirus was reduced by the Romans to the last extremity, advised the people to kill themselves universally. The people preferring to give themselves up to the enemy, the two chiefs went to seek the death they wanted, rushing furiously upon the enemy with intent to strike home but not to ward off any blow. When the Island of Gozzo was taken some years ago by the Turks, a Sicilian who had two beautiful marriageable daughters killed them both with his own hand, along with their mother who ran in to save them; that done, he sallied out of the house with a crossbow and arquebus, killed with two shots the two Turks nearest his door, and drawing his sword charged furiously among the rest, where he was quickly surrounded and cut to pieces — by that means delivering his family and himself from slavery and dishonour. The Jewish women, after circumcising their children, threw them and themselves down a precipice to escape the cruelty of Antigonus. I have been told of a man of rank in one of our prisons whose friends, hearing that he would certainly be condemned, suborned a priest to tell him — to spare him the disgrace of such a death — that the only means of his deliverance was to commend himself to such-and-such a saint under such-and-such vows, and to fast eight days together without taking any nourishment, whatever weakness or faintness he might feel. He followed their advice, and so destroyed himself before he was aware, not suspecting death or any danger in the experiment. Scribonia, advising her nephew Libo to kill himself rather than wait for the stroke of justice, told him that to keep his life only to put it after into the hands of those who within three or four days would haul him to execution was to do other people's business, and that to keep his blood for them to gratify their malice was to serve his enemies.

We read in the Bible that Nicanor, the persecutor of the law of God, having sent his soldiers to seize the good old man Razis — surnamed, for his virtue, the father of the Jews — the good man, seeing no other remedy, his gates burned down and the enemies ready to take him, chose to die nobly rather than fall into the hands of his wicked adversaries and let himself be cruelly butchered by them, contrary to the honour of his rank. He stabbed himself with his own sword, but in haste the blow had not gone home; so he ran and threw himself headlong from the top of a wall on the men below. They moved apart and made room, and he landed straight on his head. Yet, feeling still in himself some remains of life, he renewed his courage, sprang up on his feet all bloody and wounded, and making his way through the crowd to a steep rock, drew out his bowels through one of his wounds and, tearing and pulling them apart with both hands, threw them among his pursuers, all the while calling on divine vengeance for their cruelty and injustice.

Of violations of the conscience, that against the chastity of a woman is, in my opinion, the most to be avoided, since there is a certain pleasure naturally mixed with it, and for that reason her refusal cannot be perfectly complete — so that the violence seems mixed with some small consent on the part of the forced. Church history has several examples of devout persons who embraced death to secure themselves from outrages prepared by tyrants against their religion and honour. Pelagia and Sophronia, both canonised: the first threw herself with her mother and sisters into the river to avoid being forced by some soldiers; the second killed herself to avoid being raped by the Emperor Maxentius.

It may, perhaps, be an honour to us in future ages that a learned author of our day, a Parisian, has gone to great pains to persuade the ladies of our time to take any other course rather than fall into so awful a meditation as that despair. I am sorry he had never heard, that he might have included it among his other stories, the saying of a woman that was told to me at Toulouse, who had passed through the hands of some soldiers: "God be praised," she said, "that at least once in my life I have had my fill without sin." In truth, these cruelties are very unworthy of the French good nature, and, God be thanked, our air is well purged of them since this good advice came in: it is enough that they say "no" while doing it, according to the rule of the good Marot.
"Un doulx nenny, avec un doulx sourire Est tant honneste." — Marot.

History is everywhere full of people who, by a thousand routes, have exchanged a painful and tedious life for death. Lucius Aruntius killed himself, he said, to flee both the future and the past. Granius Silvanus and Statius Proximus, after being pardoned by Nero, killed themselves — either disdaining to live by the favour of so wicked a man, or so as not to be troubled at some other time to seek a second pardon, given the readiness of his nature to suspect and credit accusations against worthy men. Spargapises, son of Queen Tomyris, taken prisoner of war by Cyrus, used the first favour Cyrus showed him — ordering him untied — to kill himself, claiming no other benefit of liberty than to be revenged upon himself for the disgrace of having been captured. Boges, governor of Eion for King Xerxes, besieged by the Athenian army under Cimon, refused the terms offered (a safe return into Asia with all his wealth), unable to bear surviving the loss of a post his master had given him to keep. So, after defending the city to the last extremity, when nothing was left to eat, he first threw all the gold and everything else the enemy could plunder into the river Strymon, then ordered a great pyre lit and the throats cut of all the women, children, concubines, and servants, whose bodies he threw into the fire, and at last leaped into it himself.

Ninachetuen, an Indian lord, at the first whisper that the Portuguese Viceroy meant to strip him, with no clear cause, of his command in Malacca, in order to transfer it to the King of Campar, took this resolution: he had a scaffold built, longer than broad, supported by columns royally hung with tapestry and strewn with flowers and abundant perfumes; and when all was ready, he came out into the street in a robe of cloth of gold studded with jewels of great value, and mounted the steps to the scaffold, at one corner of which he had a pyre of aromatic wood lit. Everyone ran to see what these unusual preparations were for; whereupon Ninachetuen, with a manly but indignant air, set out how much he had served the Portuguese nation, and with how unspotted fidelity he had behaved in his charge; that, having so often, sword in hand, shown for others that honour was much dearer to him than life, he was not to abandon care for it on his own behalf; that, since fortune denied him any way of resisting the affront prepared for him, his courage at least required him to free himself from the feeling of it, and not to become a tale told by the people or a triumph to men less deserving than himself. Having said this, he leaped into the fire.

Sextilia, wife of Scaurus, and Paxaea, wife of Labeo, to encourage their husbands to escape the dangers pressing upon them — in which they had no share but conjugal affection — voluntarily sacrificed their own lives to serve them in this extreme necessity for company and example. What they did for their husbands, Cocceius Nerva did for his country, with less utility though with equal devotion: this great lawyer, flourishing in health, wealth, reputation, and favour with the emperor, had no other reason to kill himself but the bare pity of the miserable state of the Roman Republic. Nothing can be added to the beauty of the death of the wife of Fulvius, a familiar favourite of Augustus. Augustus, having discovered that he had divulged an important secret entrusted to him, received him very coldly one morning when he came to court and looked grimly at him. Fulvius returned home in despair and told his wife sorrowfully that, having fallen into this misfortune, he was resolved to kill himself; to which she answered roundly, "It is only right that you should, since after so often experiencing the looseness of my tongue you would not take warning. But let me kill myself first" — and without saying more she ran herself through the body with a sword. Vibius Virrius, despairing of the safety of his city, besieged by the Romans, and of their mercy, in the last debate of his city's senate, after many arguments to the same end, concluded that the noblest way to escape fortune was by their own hands. He told them the enemy would have them in honour, and Hannibal would feel how many faithful friends he had abandoned, and invited those who approved his advice to come to a good supper he had ready at home, where, after they had eaten well, they would all drink together of what he had prepared — "a drink," he said, "that will deliver our bodies from torments, our souls from insult, and our eyes and ears from feeling the many hateful evils the conquered suffer from cruel and implacable conquerors." He said he had arranged for proper persons to throw their bodies on a funeral pyre before his door as soon as they were dead. Many approved this high resolution, but few imitated it. Twenty-seven senators followed him, who, after having tried to drown the thought of this fatal decision in wine, ended the feast with the deadly mess; and embracing one another, after lamenting together their country's misfortune, some withdrew home to their own houses, others stayed to be burned with Vibius on his funeral pyre. All were so long in dying — the vapour of the wine having clogged the veins and so deferred the effect of the poison — that some of them came within an hour of seeing the enemy inside the walls of Capua, which was taken the next morning, and of undergoing the miseries they had at so dear a rate tried to avoid. Jubellius Taurea, another citizen of the same place, when the Consul Fulvius was returning from the shameful butchery of two hundred and twenty-five senators, called him back fiercely by name and, having stopped him, said, "Give the word that someone may dispatch me too, after the slaughter of so many others, so that you may boast of having killed a much braver man than yourself." Fulvius, dismissing him as a madman, and also having received letters from Rome censuring the inhumanity of his execution that tied his hands, Jubellius went on: "Since my country has been taken, my friends are dead, and I have with my own hands killed my wife and children to spare them the desolation of this ruin, and I am denied to die the death of my fellow citizens, let me borrow from virtue vengeance on this hated life" — and drawing a short sword he had hidden on him, he ran it through his own breast, falling backward and dying at the consul's feet.

Alexander, besieging a city of the Indies, those within, finding themselves very hard pressed, took a vigorous resolve to deny him the pleasure of his victory: they burned themselves, with the whole city, in defiance of his clemency — a new sort of war, where the enemies sought to save them, and they to destroy themselves, doing as much to make themselves sure of death as men do to secure life.

Astapa, a city of Spain, finding itself too weak in walls and defenders to withstand the Romans, the inhabitants made a heap of all their riches and furniture in the public square; and having ranged on this heap all the women and children, piled wood and other combustible matter around them to set them quickly on fire, and left fifty of their young men to carry out what they had resolved, they made a desperate sally where, for lack of strength to win, they got themselves all killed. The fifty, after massacring every living soul in the whole city and putting fire to the pile, threw themselves last into it, ending their generous freedom in an unfeeling rather than a sorrowful and shameful manner, giving the enemy to understand that, had fortune so pleased, they had as much courage to snatch victory from them as to frustrate it and render it dreadful — even mortal to those who, lured by the gleam of the gold melting in this flame, came too close: many were suffocated and burned there, kept from retreating by the crowd that pressed in behind.

The Abydeans, when pressed by King Philip, took the same resolve, but, lacking time, could not carry it out. The king, struck with horror at the rash haste of this resolution (the treasure and movables they had condemned to the flames being first secured), withdrew his soldiers and gave them three days to kill themselves in, that they might do it with more order and at greater ease — a time which they filled with blood and slaughter beyond the utmost excess of any hostile cruelty, so that not one soul was left alive that had any power to destroy itself. There are countless examples of such mass resolutions, which seem the fiercer and crueler the more universal the effect, and yet are really less so than when carried out by individuals: what argument and persuasion cannot do with single men, they can do with all, the ardour of society overriding individual judgments.

The condemned who, in the reign of Tiberius, lived to be executed, forfeited their goods and were denied burial rites; those who anticipated execution by killing themselves were buried, and were free to dispose of their estates by will.

But men sometimes covet death out of hope of a greater good. "I desire," says St. Paul, "to be with Christ," and "who shall rid me of these bands?" Cleombrotus of Ambracia, after reading Plato's Phaedo, conceived so great a desire for the life to come that, without any other occasion, he threw himself into the sea. By which it appears how improperly we call this voluntary dissolution despair — to which the eagerness of hope often inclines us, and sometimes a calm and tempered desire arising from a mature and deliberate judgment. Jacques du Chastel, bishop of Soissons, on St. Louis's foreign expedition, seeing the king and whole army about to return to France, leaving the cause of religion unfinished, took the resolve to go straight to Paradise instead. So, having taken a solemn farewell of his friends, he charged alone, in the sight of everyone, into the enemy's army, where he was at once cut to pieces. In a certain kingdom of the newly discovered world, on a day of solemn procession when the idol they worship is drawn in public on a chariot of marvellous size, besides the many seen cutting off pieces of their flesh to offer to it, there are others who throw themselves down in its path, to be crushed and broken to pieces under the heavy wheels, to obtain after death the veneration of sanctity — which is duly paid them. The death of the bishop, sword in hand, has more magnanimity in it and less sensation, since the heat of battle takes away part of the latter.

There are some governments that have taken it upon themselves to regulate the justice and the proper occasion of voluntary death. Formerly, in our city of Marseilles, a poison prepared from hemlock was kept at the public expense for those who wished to hasten their end, after first laying out before the six hundred (who were their senate) the reasons and motives of their design. It was not lawful otherwise — only by leave from the magistrate, and on just occasion, could a man do violence to himself. The same law was in use in other places too.

Sextus Pompeius, on his way to Asia, called at the isle of Cea in Negropont. It happened, while he was there — as we have it from one who was with him — that a woman of great quality, having explained to her fellow citizens why she was resolved to put an end to her life, invited Pompeius to her death to render it more honourable; an invitation he accepted. After long trying in vain with the great power of his eloquence and persuasion to turn her from her purpose, he gave way in the end to her own will. She had passed the age of ninety in a very happy state of body and mind. Lying on her bed, dressed better than usual and leaning on her elbow, "The gods," she said, "O Sextus Pompeius — and rather those I leave than those I go to seek — reward you, that you have not disdained to be both the counsellor of my life and the witness of my death. For my part, having always known the smiles of fortune, for fear that the desire of living too long may make me see a contrary face, I am going, by a happy end, to dismiss the rest of my soul, leaving behind two daughters of my body and a legion of grandchildren." Having said this, with some exhortations to her family to live in peace, she divided her goods among them, commended her household gods to her eldest daughter, and boldly took the cup that held the poison. After making her vows and prayers to Mercury to conduct her to some happy abode in the other world, she briskly swallowed the deadly draught. This done, she entertained the company with a running account of its progress and how the cold gradually seized the several parts of her body one after another; until, having at last told them it was beginning to seize on her heart and bowels, she called her daughters to do the last office and close her eyes.

Pliny tells us of a certain Hyperborean nation where, owing to the gentle temperature of the air, lives rarely end except by the voluntary surrender of the inhabitants, who, weary of and satiated with living, have the custom, at a very old age, after a good meal, of throwing themselves into the sea from the top of a certain rock set aside for that purpose. Pain and the fear of a worse death seem to me the most excusable of all incitements.
